captions: Welcome to Camday.
This lesson was written by the Camday teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 2: Human Body Systems.
When you lift a weight,
take a deep breath or feel your heart beating,
your body systems are working together.
In this unit, we'll explore the bones and muscles that move us,
the lungs that bring in oxygen, and the blood that carries it everywhere.
Our musculoskeletal system is made of bones, joints and muscles.
The bones form the skeleton.
The skeleton gives the body support and shape, allows it to move,
and protects vital organs.
The skull protects the brain, and the ribs protect the heart and lungs.
A newborn baby's bones and muscles are soft and weak,
but they grow harder and stronger with age.
Human bone is almost five times as strong
as a steel bar of the same mass!
In old age, bones and muscles may weaken again.
Bones can't bend. A joint is a place
where two or more bones meet, allowing movement.
Some joints, like those in the skull and the pelvis,
don't move at all.
They are fixed joints.
Moveable joints include ball-and-socket joints.
A ball-shaped bone end fits into a cup-shaped socket,
so the bone can move in many directions, even in a full circle.
Your shoulder and hip are ball-and-socket joints.
A hinge joint allows movement back and forth in one direction only,
like a door hinge: the door just opens and closes.
That comparison is called an analogy.
Your elbow, knee, fingers and toes have hinge joints.
This model arm has two card bones joined by a paper fastener at the elbow,
and a strip of elastic as the biceps.
Predict: will the arm bend if we push the elastic,
or only if we pull it?
Pause and decide.
Watch. First we push the elastic towards the elbow.
It just bends and nothing moves.
Then we pull the elastic, shortening it.
The lower arm lifts and the elbow bends.
Explain what you saw.
Like the elastic, a muscle can only pull, by contracting and getting shorter.
It cannot push. So muscles work in antagonistic
pairs: the biceps pulls to bend the arm,
and the triceps pulls to straighten it again.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
We have more than 600 muscles.
Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tough cords called tendons.
When a muscle contracts,
it gets shorter and fatter and pulls on the bone.
When it relaxes, it returns to its original shape.
Muscles can pull, but they can never push!
So they work in pairs that pull in opposite directions: antagonistic muscles.
In your arm, the biceps and triceps are an antagonistic pair.
To bend your arm, the biceps contracts and pulls the lower arm up,
while the triceps relaxes.
To straighten your arm, the triceps contracts and pulls the lower arm down,
while the biceps relaxes.
Your thigh muscles work the same way to bend and straighten your leg.

captions: We get oxygen from the air we breathe, using the respiratory system.
Air enters through the nose or mouth.
It travels down the trachea, which divides into two bronchi,
one for each lung.
Inside the lungs, each bronchus branches into smaller tubes called bronchioles.
Each bronchiole ends in tiny air sacs called alveoli.
Below the lungs is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle called the diaphragm.
Breathing is the physical process of moving air into and out of the lungs.
Breathing in, or inhaling: the intercostal muscles between the ribs contract,
pulling the ribs up and out.
The diaphragm contracts and moves down.
The chest gets bigger, the lungs expand, and the air pressure inside drops.
Air from outside, at higher pressure, rushes in.
Breathing out, or exhaling:
the intercostal muscles relax and the ribs move down and in.
The diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards.
The chest gets smaller, the pressure in the lungs rises,
and air is pushed out.
Room air is pumped through one tube of clear limewater.
A student gently breathes out through a straw into a second tube.
Predict: which limewater will turn milky first?
Pause and decide.
Watch. Bubbles pass through both tubes for one minute.
The limewater with breathed-out air turns milky quickly.
The other is only slightly cloudy.
Explain what you saw.
Limewater turns milky with carbon dioxide.
Breathed-out air contains about 4 percent carbon dioxide,
a hundred times more than room air,
because our cells make carbon dioxide in respiration.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
These are typical percentages of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the
air we breathe in and the air we breathe out.
The air we breathe out has less oxygen, 16 percent instead of 21,
and much more carbon dioxide: about 4 percent instead of 0.04.
Pause and decide: where did the missing oxygen go,
and where did the extra carbon dioxide come from?
The air we breathe out is different from the air we breathe in.
It contains less oxygen, 16 percent instead of 21,
and about a hundred times more carbon dioxide, 4 percent.
It also has more water vapour:
breathe on a mirror and it mists up!
Gas exchange happens in the alveoli,
which are surrounded by tiny blood vessels called capillaries.
Oxygen moves from the air in the alveoli into the blood,
and carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the alveoli,
to be breathed out.
The gases move by diffusion:
from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.
The walls of the alveoli and capillaries are only one cell thick,
so gases pass through quickly.
Breathing and respiration are different!
Breathing moves air in and out.
Respiration is a chemical process in our cells that releases energy from food.
When it uses oxygen, it's called aerobic respiration:
glucose plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water.
Starch from our food is digested into a sugar called glucose.
In the mitochondria of plant and animal cells,
a series of reactions releases its energy in a controlled, steady way,
powering life processes all the time, even while we sleep.
Germinating seeds respire too: the carbon dioxide they give off turns limewater milky.
chapters: Predict, watch, explain: what is in the air we breathe out?
Real data: air in and air out

captions: Think of the circulatory system as a transport system,
like roads and railways carrying goods around a country.
It has three parts: the heart, the blood vessels and the blood.
The heart is a double pump:
the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs,
and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body.
Arteries carry oxygenated blood away from the heart.
Veins carry deoxygenated blood back to the heart.
Tiny capillaries connect them,
delivering oxygen and nutrients to cells and taking away waste like carbon dioxide.
When blood is spun in a centrifuge, it separates into layers.
Here are the approximate percentages of each part.
More than half of blood is plasma, a yellow liquid.
Almost all the rest is red blood cells.
White blood cells and platelets make up only about 1 percent.
Pause and decide: which part of the blood transports glucose and carbon dioxide,
and which part carries oxygen?
An adult has about five litres of blood.
Spin it fast in a centrifuge, and it separates into layers:
about 55 percent is pale yellow plasma, 41 percent is red blood cells,
and a thin layer of white blood cells and platelets.
Red blood cells carry oxygen.
Their red pigment, haemoglobin,
joins with oxygen in the lungs and releases it where oxygen is low.
They have no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin,
and their biconcave disc shape gives them a large
surface area to take in and release oxygen quickly.
White blood cells defend the body.
Some wrap around pathogens and destroy them, which is called phagocytosis.
Others make antibodies that disable microorganisms.
Platelets are bits of cells that help blood clot and form scabs over cuts,
keeping pathogens out. And plasma transports blood cells, plus dissolved glucose, nutrients and carbon dioxide.
Donating blood saves lives.
We have different blood types, based partly on the antibodies in our blood.
The main blood groups are A, B, AB and O,
each either positive or negative.
People with O negative blood are universal donors:
their blood can be given safely to anyone,
so it's in high demand for emergencies.
People with AB positive blood are universal recipients:
they can receive any blood type.
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: What type of joint is the elbow,
and what movement does it allow?
Pause the video now.
Answer: A hinge joint – back and forth in one direction.
Question 2: Why do muscles work in antagonistic pairs?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Muscles can only pull, not push.
Question 3: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
Pause the video now.
Answer: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Question 4: What is the function of red blood cells?
Pause the video now.
Answer: To carry oxygen around the body.
